questions.q: What does the `@InvocableMethod` annotation let you do?
options: Expose a static Apex method as a callable action from Flow or Process Builder
Automatically encrypt a method's return value
Force a method to run asynchronously
Bypass governor limits for that specific method
questions.explain: @InvocableMethod marks a static Apex method so it appears as an available action a Flow (or Process Builder) can call directly.

questions.q: Why must an @InvocableMethod always take a List of its input wrapper class and return a List of its output wrapper class, even for a single record?
options: Because Apex cannot return a single sObject from any method
Because Flow can invoke an action against a bulk collection of records in one call, and the method must be written to bulk-process that full list rather than one record at a time
Because List is required syntax for every Apex method, with no exceptions
Because wrapper classes can only be declared as List types
questions.explain: Flow can call an action with many records in one invocation, so the List in/List out signature lets the method bulk-process the whole batch rather than being called once per record.

questions.q: Which kind of variable is NOT allowed to be marked `@InvocableVariable`?
options: A public member variable
A global member variable
A private or static member variable
A Decimal-typed member variable
questions.explain: Only public or global member variables can be marked @InvocableVariable — private, protected, static, and final members are excluded.

questions.q: What does the `label` parameter on `@InvocableVariable` control?
options: The variable's actual data type
What a Flow builder sees as that field's name inside Flow Builder's UI
Whether the field is required
The Apex access modifier applied to the field
questions.explain: label sets the display name shown to someone configuring the action in Flow Builder, defaulting to the variable's own name if omitted.

questions.q: Why can a Flow that calls an Apex action work for a System Administrator but fail for a standard user?
options: Flow actions can only ever be run by System Administrators
The running user's profile or permission set must grant access to the invoked Apex class, which a standard user may not have been given
Apex classes called from Flow are always restricted to read-only operations
Invocable methods cannot be called by any user other than the Flow's creator
questions.explain: Like other Apex entry points, a Flow-callable class requires the running user to actually have access to it through their profile or a permission set — a gap there causes failures that don't show up when testing as an admin.
